cards.front: What does a restriction enzyme do to DNA?
cards.back: It **cuts** DNA at or near a short base sequence it recognises. Each enzyme cuts only where its own recognition sequence occurs.
cards.hint: Think about what decides where an enzyme acts on a DNA molecule.

cards.front: How is a gene inserted into a plasmid to make recombinant DNA?
cards.back: 1) Cut the gene and the plasmid with the same restriction enzyme to give matching **sticky ends**. 2) The sticky ends pair by complementary base pairing. 3) **DNA ligase** seals the sugar–phosphate backbones.
cards.hint: Start with what the same enzyme does to both pieces of DNA.

cards.front: What happens in one cycle of PCR, and at what temperatures?
cards.back: **Denaturation** at about $95\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ separates the two strands. **Annealing** at $50$–$65\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ lets primers bind. **Extension** at about $72\,^{\circ}\text{C}$ lets DNA polymerase build new strands.
cards.hint: There are three stages, each at a different temperature.

cards.front: Which formula gives the number of PCR copies after a number of cycles?
cards.back: Number of copies $=$ starting copies $\times\,2^{n}$, where $n$ is the number of **cycles**. Each cycle doubles the copies, and copies have no unit.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to the copies each time the cycle repeats.

cards.front: A PCR reaction starts with 50 copies of the target region. How many copies are there after 8 cycles?

cards.back: A technique that **separates DNA fragments by size** as they move through a gel in an electric field. A stain or fluorescent label is then needed to make the fragments visible.
cards.hint: Think about how the gel behaves towards fragments of different lengths.

cards.front: Why do DNA fragments move towards the positive electrode in electrophoresis?
cards.back: DNA is **negatively charged** because of its phosphate groups, so it is attracted to the positive electrode.
cards.hint: Look at which part of each nucleotide carries the charge.

cards.front: Which DNA fragments travel further through an electrophoresis gel?
cards.back: **Short** fragments move faster and travel further. Long fragments stay nearer the wells, so saying larger fragments travel further reverses the result.
cards.hint: Think about how easily the gel mesh slows each size of fragment.

cards.front: What are the main steps in the fluorescent method of DNA sequencing?
cards.back: 1) Copy the template strand with a few labelled **chain-terminating nucleotides** present. 2) Fragments end at each base, each with its own fluorescent label. 3) Separate the fragments by size, shortest first. 4) Read the labels; the order from shortest to longest gives the base order.
cards.hint: Consider what the copied fragments look like before they are separated by size.

cards.front: Why do people disagree about growing genetically modified crops?
cards.back: Benefits include higher yields and fewer pesticide sprays. Concerns include genes spreading to wild relatives and uncertain effects on non-target organisms. Weighing these is a matter of **judgement**.
cards.hint: Think about who gains from a crop and who might bear the risks.

cards.front: Why are short tandem repeats useful for DNA profiling?
cards.back: People differ in how many times each repeat occurs, so the pattern of fragments is **almost unique** to an individual.
cards.hint: Consider what varies between people at these repeated sequences.

cards.front: What does a DNA match on its own prove at a crime scene?
cards.back: It shows the samples are **consistent with one source**, but does not prove guilt. A match alone is not proof that a suspect committed the crime.
cards.hint: Think about what other evidence a court would need alongside the profile.
